'''''Poa annua''''', or '''annual meadow grass''' (known in America more commonly as '''annual bluegrass''' or simply '''poa'''), is a widespread low-growing turfgrass in [[Temperate climate|temperate climates]]. Notwithstanding the reference to [[annual plant]] in its name, [[perennial]] [[biotype]]s do exist.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Jr |first1=J. M. Vargas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PtnRMlhbbaoC&dq=Poa+annua+annual+and+perennial+biotype&pg=PP9 |title=Poa Annua: Physiology, Culture, and Control of Annual Bluegrass |last2=Turgeon |first2=Alfred J. |date=2003-12-19 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-471-47268-1 |language=en}}</ref> 

It originated as an allopolyploid [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''[[Poa supina]]'' and ''[[Poa infirma]]''.<ref>Collins pocket guide Grasses, Sedges, Rushes and Ferns. Fitter.R, Fitter.A, Farrer.A. 1995. page 54</ref> Major [[Chromosomal rearrangement|chromosomal rearrangements]] after [[polyploidy]] have contributed to variation in [[genome size]] in ''Poa annua''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benson |first1=Christopher W. |last2=Sheltra |first2=Matthew R. |last3=Maughan |first3=Peter J. |last4=Jellen |first4=Eric N. |last5=Robbins |first5=Matthew D. |last6=Bushman |first6=B. Shaun |last7=Patterson |first7=Eric L. |last8=Hall |first8=Nathan D. |last9=Huff |first9=David R. |date=2023-06-26 |title=Homoeologous evolution of the allotetraploid genome of Poa annua L |journal=BMC Genomics |volume=24 |issue=1 |page=350 |doi=10.1186/s12864-023-09456-5 |issn=1471-2164 |pmid=37365554 |pmc=10291818 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Description==
It has a slightly creeping, fibrous rootstock. The stem grows from {{cvt|15–25|cm|0}} high. It is slightly flattened, due to being folded rather than rolled.

The [[panicle]] is open and triangular shaped, {{cvt|5–7.5|cm|0}} long. The [[spikelet]]s are stalked, [[Awn (botany)|awnless]], {{cvt|1–2|cm|1}} long when flowering, and loosely arranged on delicate paired or spreading branches.  Sometimes they are tinged purple.

The vivid green leaves are short and blunt at the tips, shaped like the [[prow]] of a small canoe. They are soft and drooping. Long sheaths clasp the stem. The leaves are smooth above and below, with finely serrated edges. Occasionally the leaves are serrated transversely.

The [[ligule]] is pointed and silvery, in comparison to common meadowgrass (''[[Poa pratensis]]''), which has a squared ligule, and ''[[Poa trivialis]]'', which has a pointed but less silvery ligule.

The leaves are smooth above and below, with finely serrated edges. Occasionally the leaves are serrated transversely.

It is in flower all year around except for severe winters.  The seeds ripen and are deposited 8 months of the year. The plant grows rapidly from seed, flowering within 6 weeks, seeding and then dying.<ref>[http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html BSBI Description] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717004923/http://www.bsbi.org.uk/identification.html |date=2011-07-17 }} retrieved 10 December 2010.</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is a common [[weed]] of cultivation, known in the Americas as annual bluegrass.<ref>{{cite web
  | last =Ohlendorf
  | first =B.
 |author2=D. W. Cudney |author3=C. L. Elmore |author4=V. A. Gibeault
  | title =Annual Bluegrass Management Guidelines--UC IPM 
  | publisher =University of California
  | date =April 2003
  | url =http://www.ipm.ucdavis.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7464.html
  | access-date =2007-09-08 }}</ref> It occurs as a common constituent of [[lawn]]s, where it is also often treated as a weed, and grows on waste ground. Many golf [[putting green]]s, including the [[Oakmont Country Club]] greens, are annual bluegrass,<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/07164/793591-382.stm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070717131632/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/07164/793591-382.stm | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 17, 2007 | work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette | title=Oakmont-inspired Stimpmeter allows USGA to accurately measure speed, consistency of putting surfaces | first=Robert | last=Dvorchak | date=2007-06-13}}</ref> although many courses have converted to [[creeping bentgrass]] (''Agrostis stolonifera'').

It has appeared on [[King George Island (South Shetland Islands)|King George Island]] in the [[Antarctic]] [[South Shetland Islands]] as an [[invasive species]],<ref>[https://www.economist.com/blogs/babbage/2012/03/antarctic-ecology Antarctic ecology: Polar invaders], [[The Economist]], Mar 6th 2012</ref> as well as on [[Australia]]'s [[subantarctic]] [[Heard Island and McDonald Islands|Heard]] and [[Macquarie Island]]s.

==Taxonomy==
''Poa annua'' is an allotetraploid hybrid species that is derived from ''[[Poa infirma|P. infirma]]'' and ''[[Poa supina|P. supina]]'' parents around 50,000 years ago.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Benson |first=Christopher W. |last2=Sheltra |first2=Matthew R. |last3=Maughan |first3=Peter J. |last4=Jellen |first4=Eric N. |last5=Robbins |first5=Matthew D. |last6=Bushman |first6=B. Shaun |last7=Patterson |first7=Eric L. |last8=Hall |first8=Nathan D. |last9=Huff |first9=David R. |date=2023-06-26 |title=Homoeologous evolution of the allotetraploid genome of Poa annua L |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10291818/ |journal=BMC genomics |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=350 |doi=10.1186/s12864-023-09456-5  |doi-access=free|issn=1471-2164 |pmc=10291818 |pmid=37365554}}</ref> ''P. annua'' and ''P. infirma'' are often confused and are believed to form a rare sterile hybrid.<ref name="grass">[http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Poa_infirma&type=treatment Grass Manual Treatment]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa annua x infirma |url=https://bsbi.org/taxa/2cd4p9h.qrg/poa-annua-x-infirma}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poa infirma – March 2020 – Somerset Rare Plants Group |url=https://www.somersetrareplantsgroup.org.uk/poa-infirma/ |access-date=2026-09-06 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
''Poa'' - derived from the [[Greek language|Greek]] name {{lang|grc|πόα}} for a type of fodder grass.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 50, 308</ref> 

''annua'' - Latin, meaning 'annual' or 'lasting a year'.<ref name="gledhill" />
